newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia welcomes cloned cattle advance as world debate rages.
newsitem.headline: Australia welcomes cloned cattle advance as world debate rages.

text.p: Australian scientists on Thursday welcomed the reported production of more than 400 clones from a single cattle embryo by Melbourne researchers, saying the breakthrough brought the cloning process to the verge of commercial production.

Australia's move into the cloning industry closely follows the cloning of an adult sheep by Scottish scientist Ian Wilmut, amid a major ethics debate in Europe on whether armies of human clones might be about to be introduced to the world.
Australia's interest is in the commercial production of cattle -- although even a welcoming local scientific community includes critics of cattle cloning.

A team including Professor Alan Trounson of Monash University, Melbourne, and Bernie Harford of Genetics Australia were said by Britain's New Scientist magazine on Thursday to have made 470 cattle clones from a single embryo. Their aim was to create a reliable herd of prize cattle.

"This is a terrific technical achievement, an order of magnitude (achieved) more than anybody else. (But) it's a production process not a research process," said Oliver Mayo of the Australian government's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO).
Scientists such as Mayo see the Trounson-Harford achievement more in the quantity of the clones produced than in the quality of the clones they have made.

But Mayo and other Australian scientists, most from the transgenics school which seeks to genetically engineer super-products rather than make clone copies of existing animals, described the Trounson-Harford breakthrough as limited.
"This is what looks like a production tool rather than a research tool," Mayo said.

Professor Laurie Piper of the Cooperative Research Centre for Premium Quality Wool, who is working to produce a Australian transgenic wool, said cloning was limited by a need to copy an existing animal.
"Embryonic cloning is widespread around the world. I don't think there's anything much new in that at all," Piper said.

While debate rages in Europe about Wilmut's cloned sheep Dolly, introduced to the world last month, concern in Australia is more about how much Trounson and his team are achieving at the high-quality end of animal-engineering and whether end-product meat will find consumer acceptance at dinner tables in Asia and the rest of the world.

Mayo believes that Trounson's real breakthrough will be to make possible the mass production of hundreds of Dolly-type clones at a time and possibly allow clone-production of hundreds of transgenically-produced animals.
"It is of commercial significance today," Mayo said.

But it produced multiple identical animals at the top of the breeding pyramid, which would inevitably lead to in-breeding, he said. "If they're all identical you've got to be very careful who you mate them with and who you mate their daughters with."
And there would be definite consumer resistance to cloned meat, he said.

"It's very natural to worry about extreme cases of things," Mayo said. "People will accept quite grotesque levels of risk if they inflict them on themselves, but they won't accept quite absurdly low risks if they come from somebody else."
